# The AI-Assisted Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."*
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* (1979) [@Box1979Robustness]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** George E. P. Box, a British statistician, coined this
aphorism about statistical models. Every model simplifies, and the working
question is whether the simplification still serves the decision at hand. A
task description, benchmark, simulator, power model, or test suite always leaves
something out. Each can still be useful when its scope and failure modes are
clear and when the decision does not reach beyond the evidence it provides.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
AI can generate more candidates and invoke more tools than an architect can
inspect by hand. How should that work be organized so that promising outputs
become defensible design decisions rather than a larger pile of plausible
results?
:::

Architecture design has always relied on a mixture of explicit artifacts and
tacit knowledge. Requirements, traces, models, register-transfer-level (RTL)
descriptions, floorplans, and review notes record part of the work. Experienced
architects supply the rest from memory. They know which workload phases count,
which model is stale, which constraint is provisional, which tool warning is
harmless, and which favorable result contradicts physical experience.

AI assistance changes the volume and pace of this work without removing those
judgments. A system can propose hundreds of candidates, write tool requests,
summarize logs, and recommend the next experiment. It can also change the
question without noticing, submit an illegal candidate, accept a clean tool
exit that measured nothing, optimize a misleading proxy, or generalize a
result beyond the conditions that produced it. A sequence of prompts and tool
calls does not reveal where any of those failures occurred.

A life cycle provides that structure. It identifies the complete set of
responsibilities needed to move from design intent to a reviewed decision,
including formulation, exploration, implementation, evaluation,
interpretation, and review. These responsibilities can repeat, overlap, and
return to earlier work. They are not six agents, six software components, or a
waterfall schedule. Their value is that each asks a different question and
leaves a different result for the next architect to inspect.

This chapter explains why those responsibilities are needed, what each must
produce, and how they fit together. The running example is one cache-capacity
decision from the mobile XR Lighthouse moonshot. The example is deliberately
small enough to follow, but the structure applies to architecture work whether
the assistance comes from one model, several agents, conventional optimization,
or a combination of AI and established engineering tools.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Explain why ad hoc prompts and tool calls are insufficient for AI-assisted
  architecture design.
- Distinguish the complete design life cycle, an iterative design loop, one
  scoped study, and the record retained for review.
- Translate broad design intent into requirements, objectives, legal
  alternatives, testable claims, and a decision the work is meant to inform.
- Distinguish an infrastructure failure, a rejected candidate, an unresolved
  comparison, a completed decision, and a budget stop.
- Explain what Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain,
  and the final Review and Decide stage must each contribute without treating
  them as a rigid sequence or a prescribed team structure.
- Preserve enough of a study for another architect to understand what was
  tried, what failed, what the results support, and what remains unresolved.
:::

## Why AI-Assisted Design Needs a Life Cycle {#sec-arch2-ontology}

Ordinary architecture work is already difficult to reconstruct after the fact.
A simulator configuration may live in one repository, the workload selection
in another, the power assumptions in a spreadsheet, and the reason for a
constraint in a reviewer's notes. Human teams bridge these gaps through shared
history and repeated discussion. An AI system has no reliable access to that
context unless the work makes it explicit.

The need becomes more acute as assistance scales. More candidates do not
automatically produce more knowledge. If ten thousand runs use the wrong
baseline, they repeat one mistake ten thousand times. If a generated RTL block
passes a narrow test but violates an unstated interface requirement, the test
has certified the wrong thing. If an optimizer finds a simulator loophole, its
best score may be the least credible candidate. Expensive simulation and EDA
runs make these errors especially costly because a bad question can consume
hours of compute before anyone discovers that the result cannot support a
decision.

Software engineering offers a useful comparison. SWE-bench gives a coding
agent a bounded issue, a known repository state, and executable tests
[@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. Architecture needs comparable discipline, but no
single test settles performance, power, area, timing, physical feasibility,
software behavior, and the system-level decision together. The relevant
feedback also arrives from tools with different costs and different limits.

Consider two teams studying the same cache with established tools. One might
use gem5, a cycle-level architecture simulator, while another uses FireSim, a
field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-accelerated full-system RTL platform
[@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Either can compare cache
sizes, misses, execution time, and energy estimates. The tool choice alone
does not say which workload phases count, whether the same baseline was rerun,
which other settings stayed fixed, or whether the result is meant to select a
design for RTL evaluation. Those declarations determine whether the teams
performed the same study.

What architects need is a common unit of work between a broad product goal and
those tools. @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl places a scoped architecture study
in that position. The study preserves the question, comparison, execution
plan, and review scope that let architects interpret otherwise disconnected
artifacts and tool results.

![**A scoped architecture study connects intent to implementation evidence.** The study contains the scope, architectural claim, execution and analysis process, and records needed for review. Iterative work may use a design loop.](images/F4d-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="85%" fig-alt="Three-layer diagram showing architecture intent and judgment above a scoped architecture study, implementation tools below it, measurements returning for review, and revision leading to a scoped finding or decision."}

Read @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl from top to bottom. The upper layer contains
the design intent, architecture models, requirements, and rationale that
establish the goals, constraints, and stakes. These inputs shape the work, but
they do not yet define a specific comparison.

The middle layer turns that intent into a piece of architecture work that can
be reviewed. Read it from left to right. The study scope names the question and
intended decision. The architectural claim states what is being investigated.
Execution and analysis define how the comparison will be performed. Results
and review record what the measurements support and connect that conclusion to
the study's decision boundary. If the results expose a faulty assumption or an
underspecified comparison, the question or claim can be revised.

The lower layer contains the tool path. Simulators and models evaluate
architectural behavior. Compilers and runtimes expose software interactions.
RTL generators turn candidates into implementations. Electronic design
automation (EDA) and signoff tools assess physical properties. The return arrow
matters as much as the downward path. Measurements flow back into the study,
where they must be interpreted against the original question, constraints,
and known tool limits.

The bar at the bottom is the payoff. A tool output is not yet an architecture
decision. The study converts a collection of outputs into a finding whose
scope is explicit and whose next action has a named owner. The figure therefore
connects intent, implementation work, and judgment without pretending that any
one of them can replace the others.

Much of the boundary of an ordinary study can remain tacit. One architect may
know that the current 2\ MB cache must be rerun because its old result used an
obsolete memory model. Another may know that initialization frames do not
represent steady operation. A simulator owner may remember which prefetcher
setting was qualified, while a project lead remembers that a 6\ MB alternative
was already rejected for area. A useful life cycle makes the assumptions that
can change the comparison, its cost, or its interpretation visible before AI
scales the work around them.

## The Complete Life Cycle

The complete life cycle has six responsibilities.

1. **Formulate** translates design intent into a question, requirements,
   objectives, legal changes, planned checks, and an intended decision.
2. **Explore** identifies alternatives worth testing and preserves enough of
   the search to show what was and was not considered.
3. **Implement** turns a candidate into valid, executable work for the relevant
   tools and establishes that the requested work actually ran.
4. **Evaluate** compares valid measurements with the declared requirements and
   objectives.
5. **Interpret and Explain** determines what the result means and whether the
   proposed mechanism accounts for it.
6. **Review and Decide** determines what the accumulated work supports, then
   advances, rejects, revises, or stops.

@fig-ontology-loop places all six responsibilities in one view. It appears
before the detailed sections so the reader can keep the whole life cycle in
mind while examining any one part.

![**A six-stage life cycle carries design intent to a reviewed decision.** Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide describe the complete responsibilities. Work can return to the responsibility that owns an inadequate result.](images/ch3-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="100%" fig-alt="Six numbered stages arranged in two rows. Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Explain, and Review and Decide carry one scoped study forward. A return path shows that review can revise the question, while other repairs return to the stage that owns the inadequate output."}

Read the top row from left to right, from Formulate through Implement, and then
the bottom row from right to left, from Evaluate through Review and Decide.
That path shows one complete passage through the work. The return arrow
illustrates a case in which review exposes a problem in the formulation and
sends the study back to revise its question. It is not the repair path for
every failure. A malformed tool request returns to Implement, while missing
observations may require another evaluation run.

The boxes divide responsibilities, not time. Exploration and implementation
may alternate thousands of times. Evaluation may reject a candidate and send
the work back to Explore. Interpretation may expose a confounding variable
that requires a new measurement. Review may narrow the question rather than
close the study. A small team can carry all six responsibilities, and a large
team can divide one responsibility among many specialists. A foundation model
or a system composed of agents may help across several boxes, but the boxes do
not prescribe its internal organization.

Four related ideas are easy to confuse.

- **Life cycle:** Names the complete responsibilities needed to move from
  intent to a defensible decision.
- **Scoped study:** Applies those responsibilities to one architecture
  question and one intended decision.
- **Design loop:** Describes an iterative path through the relevant
  responsibilities as the design changes and feedback returns.
- **Review record:** Preserves the question, attempts, observations,
  conclusions, and unresolved issues so another architect can inspect the
  work.

The life cycle is the complete map. A scoped study is one journey across it.
The design loop describes the turns taken during that journey. The review
record is what remains after each turn. None is a competing process model.

A stage boundary is useful when the work on either side can fail independently
and requires a different repair. @tbl-stage-seams applies that test to the five
adjacent boundaries.

| **Boundary** | **Different questions and outputs** | **Different inadequacy and repair** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate → Explore | Formulate asks what decision the study may support and produces a scoped plan. Explore asks which alternatives exist inside that plan and produces candidates plus a search history. | An inadequate plan returns to the question, scope, or requirements. An inadequate exploration returns to the represented design space or the method used to search it. |
| Explore → Implement | Explore asks which candidate should be tried. Implement asks whether that candidate can be expressed as a valid tool request and whether the requested work ran. | A missing or illegal candidate returns to the design space. A stale workspace, malformed request, license failure, or empty output returns to the tool setup or request. |
| Implement → Evaluate | Implement produces a valid execution record or an infrastructure failure. Evaluate produces a checked comparison. | A run that never executed cannot count against the candidate. A completed run whose result fails a declared check can. |
| Evaluate → Interpret and Explain | Evaluate asks whether the measured result meets the declared requirements and objectives. Interpretation asks what the result means and whether the proposed mechanism produced it. | A measurement problem returns to the measurement plan or candidate. A mechanism problem returns to the hypothesis, retained observations, or contrast used to test it. |
| Interpret and Explain → Review and Decide | Interpretation produces a supported, revised, or contradicted account. Review asks what that account and the checked result permit the study to conclude. | An incomplete explanation returns to the hypothesis or study. An insufficient record narrows the conclusion, reopens a named responsibility, or stops honestly. |

: **Stage boundaries separate different questions and repairs.** Read each row
across. When neither the question nor the repair differs, adjacent
responsibilities can be combined for that project. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[20,41,39]"}

## From Intent to Requirements and a Design Decision

Formulation begins with intent, but intent is not yet a testable architecture
problem. The Lighthouse goal asks for a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V mobile XR
subsystem. It leaves open whether the relevant intervention belongs in the
instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, accelerator, memory
system, compiler, runtime, or their interfaces. It also leaves open what
evidence would justify acting on a proposal.

Refinement preserves that intent while making it progressively testable. A
system-level goal becomes workload and user-facing requirements. Those
requirements become architecture choices and interface obligations. An ISA or
hardware-software interface then constrains what software may assume and what
hardware must provide. An implementation finally exposes measurable timing,
power, area, and correctness properties. Each refinement can add detail, but
it should not silently change the original goal.

@fig-ontology-chain shows the dependencies that connect a scoped question to a
decision. This is not a second life cycle. It is a check that the artifacts
created across the life cycle continue to refer to the same design intent.

![**Formulation fixes the question and leaves later work open.** The scope and architectural claim are declared first. Later work supplies represented state, an approach, executable requests, qualified results, review, and a named decision owner.](images/F4-ontology-chain){#fig-ontology-chain width="85%" fig-alt="A common structure connecting a scoped architecture study and its architectural claim to represented state, tools, an execution and analysis process, results, review, a named decision owner, and a scoped finding or decision."}

Read the five numbered links from top to bottom. Scope fixes the question,
baseline, design space, requirements, and intended decision. The claim states
the expected mechanism and effect and what could rule them out. Representation
makes the relevant state and permitted changes inspectable. Tools and their
interfaces make selected work executable. Execution and analysis perform the
work. Results and review then determine which finding or decision the work can
support. A red return path applies when later work shows that the question or
claim itself needs revision.

The XR example narrows the broad moonshot to one pre-RTL cache decision. The
question is which, if either, of two larger L2 capacities should advance to RTL
evaluation. @tbl-bounded-study-contract records the plan before any search
method is chosen. The values are illustrative. Their purpose is to show which
declarations make the comparison and its limits inspectable.

| **Declaration** | **Mobile XR cache study** |
| --- | --- |
| Question | Which, if either, of the 3\ MB and 4\ MB L2 candidates should advance to RTL evaluation for the declared XR workload? |
| Comparator | The current 2\ MB L2 baseline. Both larger candidates are compared against the same rerun baseline. |
| Scope | One cache-capacity decision inside the compute subsystem. Cache policy, network-on-chip topology, compiler, runtime, and the rest of the memory system remain fixed. |
| Permitted changes | L2 capacity may take the values 2\ MB, 3\ MB, or 4\ MB. No other architecture parameter may change in this study. |
| Hard constraints | Modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power must not exceed 3\ W. The cache macro must not exceed 1.5\ mm^2^, and its modeled access time must not exceed the 2.5\ ns allocation used by the 2\ GHz microarchitecture. Required thermal and resistive voltage-drop (IR-drop) review remains independent. |
| Objectives and tradeoffs | Reduce 99th-percentile frame time while limiting added power and area. A candidate that improves tail latency at higher cost remains a tradeoff alternative rather than an automatic winner. |
| Conditions | Workload snapshot `XR-TRACE-A`, including stable frame identifiers and boundaries; RISC-V software image `SW-BASE-A`; and recorded versions of the cycle-level simulator, cache model, power model `PM-A`, static random-access memory (SRAM) model `SRAM-A`, and process, voltage, and temperature assumptions `PVT-A`. |
| Planned measurements and checks | Measure 99th-percentile frame time, cache misses by classification including capacity misses, dynamic and leakage power, macro area, and access time while retaining stable frame identifiers. Estimate the frame-time reduction and its 95% interval with paired block resampling over matched contiguous frame groups from the baseline and candidate together. A capacity advances only if its physical checks pass and that interval relative to 2\ MB lies above zero. |
| Budget | Four cycle-level executions in total, including reruns after infrastructure failures, plus one SRAM timing, area, and power evaluation per declared capacity. No RTL synthesis or physical signoff is included. |
| Stopping conditions | Stop when the intended decision is resolved, all permitted capacities are exhausted, the run budget is spent, or a required input or measurement remains unavailable. |
| Intended decision | Recommend at most one cache capacity for a later RTL study. This plan does not authorize implementation, signoff, tapeout, or a product commitment. |
| Exclusions | Cache policy, prefetching, coherence, network-on-chip changes, compiler changes, software scheduling, full floorplanning, thermal signoff, IR-drop signoff, security, reliability, and product-level cost. |

: **A scoped plan declares the comparison before a method is chosen.** Read the
first four rows as the question and legal design space, the next four as the
requirements and planned observations, and the final four as the study's cost
and decision boundary. {#tbl-bounded-study-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Hard constraints and tradeoff objectives play different roles. A hard
constraint rules out a candidate. A design that misses timing is not rescued
by excellent energy efficiency. An objective ranks or compares candidates that
remain feasible. Power, area, latency, and implementation effort may pull in
different directions, so exploration may return a Pareto set rather than one
universally best design. A Pareto alternative is one that cannot improve one
declared objective without worsening another.

The table's tail-latency objective is intentional. Real-time XR is judged by
whether frames meet their deadlines, not only by average throughput. A cache
that improves mean instructions per cycle while lengthening the slowest frames
can be a system-level regression. The planned comparison therefore uses
99th-percentile frame time and paired block
resampling[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c03] rather than treating two complete
executions as the statistical sample.

[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c03]: **Paired block resampling** estimates
uncertainty by repeatedly selecting matched groups of nearby observations from
the baseline and candidate together. Keeping neighboring frames in blocks
preserves short-range dependence, while pairing ensures that each comparison
uses corresponding workload intervals rather than unrelated samples.

An architectural claim makes the expected result falsifiable.

> **Architectural claim.** An architectural claim states the proposed
> mechanism, expected outcome, scenario, comparator, alternatives,
> requirements, and evidence that would count against it.

For this study, the claim is that at least one larger L2 reduces
99th-percentile frame time relative to the 2\ MB baseline because it removes
capacity misses while remaining inside the declared power, area, and timing
constraints. The claim does not assume that fewer misses necessarily reduce
frame time. It makes that connection something the measurements must test.

A cheap analytic check can reject an impossible claim before any simulator is
invoked. If the frames that set the tail spend 18 percent of their latency
stalled on L2 capacity misses, eliminating every one of those stalls can
recover at most that fraction for those observations. This Amdahl-style upper
bound [@HillMarty2008Amdahl] cannot select a cache size, but it can reject a
claim that asks the named mechanism for more improvement than the workload
contains.

Requirements also need units and conditions. A 3\ W limit and a 2\ GHz target
do not identify the power components, workload state, process corner, voltage,
temperature, or guardband under which they must hold. Coupled effects such as
cache banking, interconnect distance, floorplan blockage, power delivery, and
temperature remain visible whenever they could reverse the comparison.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Mars Climate Orbiter and the units nobody checked"}
**The claim.** The Mars Climate Orbiter navigation team consumed an impulse
value whose interface specification required newton-seconds
[@MCOMishapBoard1999].

**The gap.** Ground software supplied pound-force seconds. Each component ran,
but nothing checked the value where it crossed the interface. The 4.45
conversion error accumulated until the reconstructed closest approach was 57
km, below the planned 226 km and the estimated survivable minimum of 80 km.

**The lesson.** A written requirement is not operational until the work names
its units and conditions and assigns a check at the interface where the value
is consumed. Architecture tool paths cross many such interfaces, and a clean
run cannot repair a missing check.
:::

## Explore Alternatives

Exploration asks which alternatives are worth testing inside the declared
design space. It does not decide whether a candidate works. It produces legal
candidates, the reason they were selected, and a record of the region that was
searched or pruned.

The simplest search method is often the right one. The XR study has only three
legal cache capacities, so direct enumeration is clearer than an elaborate
learned method. Larger spaces may justify prediction, generation,
optimization, or combinations of them. The life-cycle responsibility remains
the same even when the method changes. Exploration must stay inside the legal
space and expose enough of its selection process for a reviewer to understand
why some candidates received expensive evaluation while others did not.

Legal does not mean independent. Increasing cache capacity can change access
time, banking, interconnect distance, leakage, floorplan pressure, and the
software-visible benefit of another optimization. Exploration therefore works
with coupled alternatives rather than a bag of unrelated parameters. It must
also preserve interface and software assumptions so that a candidate does not
win by changing something the study declared fixed.

Cheap checks belong as early as possible. The Amdahl-style upper bound can
discard a claim whose mechanism cannot deliver the required gain. An SRAM model
can reject a capacity that cannot meet the cycle allocation before a
cycle-level run is spent. These checks prune candidates, but they do not
substitute for later measurements of the surviving designs.

Multiple objectives complicate the meaning of "best." If the 3\ MB candidate
has lower tail latency and the 2\ MB baseline has lower area, neither dominates
the other on those two objectives. Exploration should preserve such Pareto
alternatives until the architect applies the declared tradeoff. Collapsing
power, area, performance, and risk into an undeclared scalar score hides the
decision rather than automating it.

For the XR study, Explore produces two new candidates, 3\ MB and 4\ MB, plus
the rerun 2\ MB baseline. It may record that a larger capacity was excluded by
the declared space or a cheap timing estimate. It has not yet shown that any
candidate is correctly implemented, that any measurement is valid, or that
one should advance.

## Implement a Testable Candidate

Implementation turns a selected candidate into executable work. In an
AI-assisted setting, this may mean generating RTL, modifying simulator
parameters, constructing a workload, writing a compiler transformation, or
preparing a sequence of EDA tool commands. The essential result is not code or
a command file by itself. It is a candidate that the intended tools can
actually test under the declared conditions.

Each tool request must preserve the candidate's identity and the study state.
For the XR cache study, the request must name the cache parameters, baseline
software image, workload trace, clocks, process assumptions, and expected
outputs. It must also confirm that the tool used them. A syntactically valid
configuration can still select the wrong top level, reuse stale constraints,
or skip the workload region that defines the comparison.

This creates a crucial distinction between an infrastructure failure and a
candidate failure. A crash, license timeout, stale workspace, malformed timing
constraint, empty netlist, or clean exit that analyzed no paths says that the
requested test did not run correctly. It says nothing about the quality of the
candidate. Only a valid execution can produce a result that later rejects a
design.

For the XR study, the 2\ MB, 3\ MB, and 4\ MB capacities must become valid SRAM
model and cycle-level simulator requests. If an inexpensive SRAM check runs
first, Implement must confirm that its area and access-time outputs describe
the intended capacity and conditions before passing them to Evaluate. The
detailed mechanics of tool isolation, retry, recovery, and interface design
belong to environment engineering. At the life-cycle level, the handoff is
simple. Either the intended work ran and produced qualified outputs, or the
attempt remains an infrastructure failure.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The tool reported a chip that did not exist"}
**The trap.** An automated search reports 0.0\ W and 0.0\ mm^2^ with a
successful tool exit.

**What happened.** The request selected no valid top-level design and omitted
the primary clock. Elaboration contained none of the expected instances,
timing analysis had no constrained paths, and a downstream parser substituted
zeros for absent power and area fields.

**The result.** This is an infrastructure failure, not a breakthrough and not
a rejected candidate. A useful implementation check confirms that the expected
clocks, instances, paths, and outputs exist before evaluation interprets their
numbers.

This is a composite of a recurring tool-flow failure pattern rather than one
published incident.
:::

## Evaluate the Candidate

Evaluation begins only after implementation establishes that the intended work
ran. It compares the returned measurements with the requirements, objectives,
and validity conditions declared during formulation. The result is not merely
a score. It states which checks passed, which failed, which remain unresolved,
and how much confidence the available measurements justify.

The XR study first applies hard physical checks. A cache macro outside the
1.5\ mm^2^ area limit, beyond the 2.5\ ns access-time allocation, or above the
3\ W subsystem envelope is rejected even if it improves frame time. A feasible
candidate then faces the tail-latency comparison with the rerun 2\ MB baseline.
A reduction in capacity misses does not substitute for a resolved frame-time
result because the claim names both the mechanism and the system-level outcome.

Cost and fidelity shape the order of evaluation. An analytic estimate or SRAM
model may cheaply reject a candidate before a cycle-level run. Simulation may
then estimate workload behavior before RTL synthesis or physical analysis.
This escalation conserves expensive evidence for the candidates that need it.
It does not make the lower-fidelity checks unimportant. Their assumptions and
error bounds determine which candidates survive long enough to reach the
expensive tools.

Higher fidelity strengthens an answer to the declared question, but it does
not widen the decision the study may support. A successful cycle-level
simulation does not authorize RTL implementation if the study promised only a
recommendation for further evaluation. Likewise, an RTL result does not waive
thermal, IR-drop, reliability, or product review that the study excluded.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A 3\ W result is only one part of the decision"}
**Context.** A power result becomes useful only when a reviewer can see which
workload, candidate, tool state, software assumptions, and power components it
describes.

**In this study.** If a run reports 2.94\ W under the recorded conditions, that
value satisfies only the declared power check. The intended decision still
depends on a resolved tail-latency comparison and later independent physical
review. Passing one check cannot resolve another.
:::

An evaluation can therefore end in several legitimate states. A valid result
may reject a candidate. The measurement may be too uncertain to distinguish
two candidates. The run budget may expire before the comparison resolves.
Required data may be unavailable. These are not interchangeable failures. Each
state determines a different next action and must remain visible to review.

## Interpret and Explain the Result

Evaluation asks whether a result clears the declared checks. Interpretation
asks what the result means, while explanation asks whether the proposed
mechanism accounts for it. A favorable number can pass evaluation and still
fail this responsibility.

Suppose the 3\ MB cache reduces capacity misses and improves
99th-percentile frame time. The result is consistent with the claim, but it
does not yet establish the mechanism. The larger cache may also change hit
latency, memory-level parallelism, prefetch behavior, or contention. Stable
frame identifiers, miss classifications, and relevant pipeline or memory
telemetry let the architect connect the measured outcome to a physical account
instead of relying on a plausible narrative.

Gupta and colleagues provide a useful warning. They used an evolutionary
coding agent to write last-level cache replacement policies for ChampSim
[@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim; @GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent]. One generated policy appeared
to improve instructions per cycle by bypassing writes that then disappeared
from the modeled memory system. The simulator score improved, but the gain did
not come from a valid cache mechanism. Inspection and targeted tests exposed
the loophole.

That case does not mean every result needs an elaborate causal proof. It means
that a metric and its mechanism are different claims. A direct physical check
may explain a simple violation. More coupled behavior may require a contrast,
counterfactual, or ablation.^[An ablation removes or replaces one component
while holding the rest of the comparison fixed to test whether the result
depends on it. One-at-a-time ablations can miss interactions among components.]
The planned level of explanation should match the consequence of the decision
and the ways the evaluation setup can be exploited.

The needed observations should be chosen before the expensive run whenever
possible. A top-line score cannot recover miss classifications, pipeline
events, or per-frame histories that the run discarded. Treating interpretation
as part of the life cycle therefore changes evaluation itself. The run retains
the observations needed to test the mechanism rather than waiting for review
to discover that the explanation requires another full execution.

Interpretation also includes uncertainty and scope. A result from one workload,
software stack, process assumption, or simulator version does not automatically
generalize to another. The explanation should state what is known, what remains
plausible but untested, and what observation would contradict the current
account. Fluent prose from an AI system can help organize this reasoning, but
it cannot replace the architectural measurements that support it.

For the XR study, this responsibility determines whether reduced capacity
misses occur in the frames that shape the tail and whether that reduction
accounts for the observed frame-time change. It may support both the mechanism
and the outcome, support only one, or leave both unresolved. Those distinctions
constrain what review can conclude.

## Review, Decide, Revise, or Stop

Review brings the scoped plan and all subsequent work back together. The
architect asks whether the legal alternatives were explored adequately,
whether the intended tools ran, whether the measurements satisfy the declared
checks, whether the explanation is credible, and whether the accumulated work
supports the intended decision.

The result is not always approval. Review may advance one candidate, reject a
candidate, request another comparison, revise the question, narrow the
conclusion, or stop because the budget or available information is exhausted.
An honest unresolved result is a useful outcome when the record makes clear
why the question remains open.

The completed stage narratives can now be read as one compact set of
inspectable handoffs (@tbl-stage-contracts).

| **Stage** | **Receives** | **Produces and checks** | **Repair and handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate | Product intent, a design question, known requirements, and applicable downstream checks. | A scoped plan whose question, comparator, objectives, constraints, conditions, measurements, budget, stop, decision, and exclusions agree. | Repair the question or scope. Hand the plan to Explore without choosing a method prematurely. |
| Explore | The scoped plan and a represented set of legal changes. | One or more legal candidates, or a record that no candidate remains expressible or clears a declared cheap prerequisite. | Repair the design space or search approach. Hand a named candidate and its selection history to Implement. |
| Implement | A candidate, requested tool work, budget, and required inputs. | An execution record showing the requested work ran on the intended state, or a recorded infrastructure failure showing that it did not. | Repair the request or tool setup. Hand completed tool returns to Evaluate. Never treat an unevaluated candidate as rejected. |
| Evaluate | Completed tool returns, comparator, planned metrics, thresholds, and validity conditions. | A comparison stating which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved, together with the observations needed for interpretation. | Repair the measurement plan, rerun within budget, or reject the candidate on a declared check. |
| Interpret and Explain | The checked result, proposed mechanism, and retained observations. | An account supported, revised, or contradicted by a declared contrast, ablation, or direct physical reason. | Repair the hypothesis or request missing observations. Hand the result and mechanism status to review. |
| Review and Decide | The scoped plan and cumulative record from all prior work. | A decision within the declared scope, a narrower conclusion, a named revision, or an honest stop with unresolved questions. | Reopen the work that owns the missing result or close the study. Preserve the reason for the action. |

: **Each responsibility produces something another architect can inspect.** The
table summarizes inputs, outputs, and repair paths without prescribing a
specific model, method, tool interface, or team organization.
{#tbl-stage-contracts tbl-colwidths="[15,25,34,26]"}

Read down the first column to follow one complete passage through the work.
Then read across a row to see what must change before the next responsibility
can begin. The Implement and Evaluate rows give the decisive contrast. A tool
request must first establish that the intended work ran before its numbers can
pass or fail an architecture check. Review uses these handoffs to decide where
any missing result must return.

Authority should be assigned by action rather than by giving a system one
overall label such as autonomous. A system may be allowed to propose a
candidate, execute a declared test, reject a candidate when a mechanical check
fails, or recommend a next step. Waiving a requirement and committing the
project to a costly or irreversible action are different rights. They remain
with named people who accept the residual risk. This distinction lets AI take
initiative without allowing it to enlarge its own authority.

When work iterates, the design loop keeps each change connected to the original
question and the next decision. Established agile hardware practices, including
the Chisel ecosystem, provide one lineage for this kind of iteration
[@Izraelevitz2017Chisel]. @fig-design-loop shows the information that must
remain connected even as the implementation practice changes.

![**An iterative architecture study keeps each tool run connected to the question and decision.** An architect or method reads the recorded state, makes a permitted change, runs the relevant tools, interprets the returned feedback, and records the next action.](images/F3-design-loop){#fig-design-loop width="85%" fig-alt="A design loop within a scoped architecture study. Recorded state, a permitted change, tool feedback, review, and the next decision remain connected."}

Read @fig-design-loop from left to right. The loop starts with the current
design state, including the workload, baseline, requirements, and prior
results. An architect or method makes a permitted change. The relevant tools
return feedback from simulation, measurement, or physical analysis. That
feedback becomes useful only when it remains connected to the candidate,
conditions, provenance, and known tool limits. Review then applies the declared
checks and decides whether to accept, reject, revise, continue, or stop.

The return path is the reason to call it a loop. A rejected 4\ MB cache may send
exploration toward a different capacity or close that part of the design
space. A tool failure returns to implementation without changing the candidate.
An unexplained frame-time gain may request additional telemetry or an ablation.
A revised product requirement can reopen formulation. The recorded reason for
the return prevents the next turn from repeating the same work blindly.

The lower bar in the figure separates fidelity from authority. A study may
move from a proxy to simulation and then to a higher-fidelity check, usually at
increasing cost. More faithful evidence can strengthen the answer to the
declared question. It cannot expand who may commit the design or waive an
independent requirement.

### A Record Another Architect Can Review {#sec-design-loop-card}

A cumulative review record makes those distinctions inspectable.

> **Study record.** The cumulative account of one scoped architecture study.
> It retains the plan, stage outputs, failed or unevaluated work, unresolved
> questions, stopping reason, and supported decision, with links to the
> detailed artifacts needed for review or replay.

The existing design-loop card is a compact index into that record.

> **Design-loop card.** A short guide to one architecture study. It points to
> the question, scope, stage outputs, results, stop, and decision. Detailed
> design state, tool returns, and replay artifacts remain in linked records.

Model cards provide a precedent for concise disclosure
[@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards], but architecture studies must also retain design
changes, tool conditions, physical checks, rejected alternatives, and a
decision boundary. @fig-filled-design-loop-card shows how the card separates
those concerns for a filled system-level example.

![**A filled study card separates support from decision.** The top band names the claim under review. The paired fields connect intent and scope to methods, checks, results, and rejected alternatives. The final row keeps what the results support separate from the accountable decision.](images/F4b-design-loop-card-example){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="96%" fig-alt="A filled study card for an XR accelerator comparison. A claim under review appears above twelve paired fields covering intent, task, design space, representation, environment, method role, feedback budget, evidence, failed and rejected alternatives, rejection checks and authority, what the evidence supports, and the accountable decision."}

Read the card from the claim at the top through the paired fields below. Intent,
task, and design space establish the comparison. Representation, environment,
and method role state how the study can act. Feedback budget, results, failed
work, and rejection checks record what the study actually tested. The final
row separates the supported finding from the accountable decision so that a
promising result cannot silently become a product commitment.

At formulation, the XR cache study fills the fields it already knows and leaves
later entries visibly open (@tbl-design-loop-card-fields).

| **Field** | **The cache study's entry at formulation** |
| --- | --- |
| Intent | Improve XR subsystem efficiency without weakening the declared physical checks. |
| Task | Decide which, if either, of the 3\ MB and 4\ MB L2 candidates should advance to RTL evaluation. |
| Design space | The 2\ MB baseline and 3\ MB and 4\ MB candidates, with all other architecture choices fixed. |
| Representation | Required state is named, but its durable form and relationships remain open. |
| Environment | The required simulator, power, and SRAM model work is named. Exact interfaces, isolation, and recovery remain open. |
| Method role | No AI method is selected. Direct enumeration is an available approach because the declared space is small. |
| Feedback budget | Four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns, plus one SRAM timing, area, and power evaluation per declared capacity. The budget is available but not yet spent. |
| Evidence | Awaiting execution. Planned results include cache-miss classifications, power, area, access time, tail latency, the interval around the frame-time comparison, and links to observations needed to test the mechanism. |
| Failed runs and rejected alternatives | None yet. Later records must distinguish infrastructure failures, unevaluated candidates, and candidates rejected by a declared check. |
| Rejection checks and authority | Power, area, access time, and tail-latency checks are declared. They can reject a candidate within this study. Authority to waive later thermal or IR-drop review is not granted here. |
| What the evidence supports | Open until valid tool returns are evaluated and the proposed mechanism is tested. |
| Accountable decision | Open. Possible outcomes are to advance at most one candidate, reject candidates on declared checks, narrow the conclusion, revise a named part of the study, or stop honestly. Product commitment remains outside this study. |

: **The card indexes the review record rather than replacing it.** Read the
first rows as the question and setup, the middle rows as the work performed,
and the final rows as the checks, supported conclusion, and decision. An
unfinished field identifies unfinished work rather than a formatting defect.
{#tbl-design-loop-card-fields tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The card makes five outcomes visibly different. An infrastructure failure
means the intended test did not run. A rejected candidate means a valid result
failed a declared check. An unresolved comparison means the available
measurements cannot settle the question. A budget stop means the study ended
before resolution because its declared resources were exhausted. A completed
decision means every required result supports one of the actions the plan
authorized.

The public [YAML template](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/design-loop-card/template.yaml),
[Markdown template](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/design-loop-card/template.md),
and [JSON schema](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/schemas/design-loop-card.v2.schema.json)
provide machine-readable forms. Validation can check the shape and links of a
card. It cannot decide that the engineering work behind the card was adequate.
That remains a review judgment.

## Open Research Questions

The life cycle and cumulative record remain proposals to test rather than
rules to assume.

### Useful Structure Without Bureaucracy

**What is the smallest set of declarations that prevents an AI system, tool, or
reviewer from changing the design question without noticing?** Removing a
declaration should produce an observable failure, not merely violate a
preference for more documentation.

**When can adjacent responsibilities be combined without hiding the source of
a failure?** Independent projects could test whether differences in questions,
outputs, and repair paths predict which boundaries remain useful.

**How should the structure change as a decision becomes more expensive or less
reversible?** Early exploration and tapeout commitment should not require the
same record, but they should preserve a traceable relationship.

### Repair, Learning, and Generalization

**How should a study route repair when several parts are inadequate at once?**
A stale workload, weak representation, failed tool request, and unresolved
metric can coexist. Repair needs an order that does not mistake the most
visible failure for the first one to fix.

**Which failed attempts should be retained so that future systems learn without
overgeneralizing a rejection?** A candidate rejected under one workload,
process, or software stack may become useful when those conditions change.

**How can an architecture team tell when a successful result transfers to a
new workload, interface, technology, or design layer?** The life cycle exposes
the original scope, but methods for efficient revalidation remain open.

### Review at Machine-Generated Scale

**How much of a high-volume study must remain replayable?** Preserving every
intermediate artifact may cost more than it saves, while preserving only the
final candidate can make the stopping reason and failed alternatives impossible
to inspect.

**Which checks can be automated without allowing the system to certify its own
assumptions?** Tool validity and threshold checks may be mechanical, while
workload relevance and acceptable residual risk remain judgment.

**How should architects review explanations produced by systems that also
selected the candidates and measurements?** Independent tests, adversarial
review, and separation of decision rights may be needed when one system shapes
the entire argument.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Organize the work before scaling it"}
AI can accelerate candidate generation, tool execution, and analysis, but it
cannot repair an unstated question or decide what its own results are allowed
to authorize. Make the complete design responsibility visible before
increasing the volume of work.
:::

The AI-assisted design life cycle organizes the complete path from intent to a
reviewed architecture decision. Formulate turns a broad goal into testable
requirements, objectives, legal alternatives, and an intended decision.
Explore finds candidates inside that space. Implement makes a candidate
testable and distinguishes valid work from infrastructure failure. Evaluate
applies the declared checks. Interpret and Explain connect the measured result
to an architecture mechanism and its limits. Review and Decide determine what
the cumulative work supports and whether to advance, reject, revise, or stop.

These responsibilities are neither a waterfall nor an agent architecture.
They can repeat, overlap, and return to the work that needs repair. Their
purpose is to keep different failures from collapsing into one unsuccessful
run. A malformed invocation is not a rejected design. A favorable score is not
an explanation. A higher-fidelity measurement is not broader authority. A
budget stop is not a completed decision.

The XR cache example showed how one scoped study uses the complete life cycle.
Its broad system goal became a narrow decision about which cache capacity, if
any, should advance to RTL evaluation. Hard constraints remained separate from
tradeoff objectives. Tail latency stayed connected to the real-time workload.
Tool requests had to establish that the intended design ran before any number
could reject a candidate. The final record preserved open questions and
decision limits rather than filling them in after the fact.

The durable lesson is larger than the example. AI-assisted architecture design
needs a way to preserve intent as work crosses models, methods, software,
hardware descriptions, simulators, and physical tools. The life cycle supplies
that common structure. It lets AI do more of the work without allowing the
speed or fluency of the system to become a substitute for engineering
judgment.
